name: Oil Fields
description: Iran’s oil-field development combines efforts to sustain established production with projects in the West Karun region near Iraq. Contracts and announced capacity targets describe development intentions; they do not by themselves establish completed facilities or sustained output.

seo.title: Iran’s Oil Fields: West Karun and Development Evidence | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s West Karun oil developments and why signed contracts, production capacity, and sustained field output require separate evidence.

content.heading: A development frontier near Iraq
content.content: West Karun is an important focus of Iran’s oil-development plans. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s October 2024 assessment identifies Azadegan, Yadavaran, and Yaran among projects in this region along the Iraqi border. It also reports slow progress amid financing and technology constraints. This is a dated assessment of development conditions, rather than confirmation of operating conditions at the editorial cutoff. [s1]

content.heading: What a development contract establishes
content.content:
On March 17, 2024, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported that the National Iranian Oil Company, the national upstream oil company commonly abbreviated NIOC, signed contracts with domestic companies for projects at Azadegan, Azar 2, Soumar, Saman, Delavaran, and Masjed-Soleiman. The report placed the combined contract value at approximately $13 billion. That figure describes the announced agreements; it is not evidence that the full amount was spent or that the intended production increases were achieved. [s2]

IRNA situated the signing shortly before Oil Nationalization Day, which commemorates Iran’s assertion of control over its oil industry in 1951. This framing shows how upstream investment announcements can carry historical and national significance alongside their commercial purpose. The report remains an institutional account of a signing ceremony, rather than an independent evaluation of project delivery. [s2]

content.heading: Reading field announcements carefully
content.content:
EIA reported that production began at Jufair and Sepehr in March 2024. A reported startup is a different milestone from a contract award, but neither establishes a comparable annual production history. [s1]

For readers following these developments, the useful distinction is between a project’s legal commitment, its first production, and its sustained operating performance. The inspected sources establish selected announcements and startups; they do not support a complete field-by-field account through October 2026. [s1][s2]

name: Gas Fields
description: South Pars is central to Iran’s gas-field development and domestic energy supply. Its development history illustrates the separate challenges of reservoir production, processing infrastructure, investment, and maintaining output as reservoir pressure declines.

seo.title: Iran’s Gas Fields: South Pars and Development Challenges | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore South Pars through documented development agreements, production milestones, pressure-management challenges, and dated disruption reports.

content.heading: South Pars and the development of gas supply
content.content: South Pars is Iran’s largest non-associated gas field: its gas production is not dependent on extracting oil from an oil field. EIA’s October 2024 assessment identifies successive South Pars developments as an important source of Iran’s gas-production growth. It also describes pressure decline and investment constraints as challenges to maintaining future output. [s1]

content.heading: Phase 11: an agreement and its changing assumptions
content.content:
A development phase is a project within the larger field. In July 2017, Total announced an agreement with the National Iranian Oil Company for South Pars Phase 11. The announcement envisaged gas supplying Iran’s domestic market and a later development stage involving offshore compression. These were project plans, not evidence that the facilities subsequently operated as described. [s2]

In May 2018, following the United States’ announced withdrawal from the nuclear agreement, Total said it would have to unwind its involvement unless it received a project-specific sanctions waiver. Its statement directly documents the company’s position and the conditions it placed on continued participation. It does not establish the eventual performance of the replacement development arrangements. [s3]

EIA subsequently reported that Phase 11 partially entered production in August 2023. The sequence illustrates why the original agreement, a participant’s withdrawal position, and a later production milestone must be read as distinct events. [s1]

content.heading: The field and its onshore facilities
content.content:
Reporting about South Pars can refer to the offshore resource or to facilities treating its gas on land. S&P Global reported on June 15, 2025, that fires at the onshore South Pars Phase 14 and Fajr Jam gas-treatment plants had been contained following attacks. Its report explicitly said there was no update on whether the plants had returned to service. A contained fire therefore cannot be treated as proof of restored gas supply. [s4]

The Associated Press reported further attacks affecting the South Pars gas and associated petrochemical complex in April 2026. Its account connected the complex with domestic energy use and chemical production. That reporting establishes additional disruption concerns, but does not provide an audited assessment of field-wide production or subsequent recovery through October. [s5]

name: Refineries
description: Iran’s petroleum-processing infrastructure includes crude-oil refineries and facilities processing gas-field condensate. Reported capacity, actual throughput, and the production of particular fuels measure different aspects of this system.

seo.title: Iran’s Refineries: Capacity, Condensate and Fuel Supply | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s refinery capacity statistics, the role of condensate processing, and the difference between installed capacity and available fuel supply.

content.heading: Different facilities, different measures
content.content: Iran’s petroleum-processing system includes crude-oil distillation and condensate processing. EIA identifies Persian Gulf Star as a facility processing condensate from South Pars and describes a new distillation unit added at Abadan in March 2023. Its assessment also notes continued gasoline imports despite processing investments. More installed processing equipment does not, by itself, demonstrate that domestic demand for every fuel is met. [s1]

content.heading: A consistent published capacity series
content.content:
OPEC’s 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin reports Iran’s refinery capacity at 2,201 thousand barrels per day in 2020, rising to 2,237 thousand barrels per day in 2022 and remaining at that reported level through 2024. The accompanying series preserves those published values. It measures capacity rather than actual refinery intake or fuel production. [s2]

The complete table footnotes could not be inspected because direct retrieval of the PDF failed. Consequently, the series should be treated as OPEC’s reported capacity measure, without assuming that its coverage matches another publisher’s crude-distillation or condensate-processing totals. It should not be used to calculate a utilization rate against a differently defined throughput series. [s2]

content.title: Iran’s reported refinery capacity, 2020–2024
content.interpretation: OPEC reports a small increase between 2020 and 2022, followed by unchanged capacity through 2024. These figures do not establish throughput, product quality, or subsequent operating availability.

content.heading: Why precise facility identification matters
content.content: Fuel depots, oil refineries, and gas-treatment plants should be distinguished when assessing disruption. On June 15, 2025, S&P Global reported a fire at the Shahran storage depot while describing the nearby Tehran oil refinery as unaffected and operating normally, citing Iran’s oil ministry news service. The same report separately discussed fires at gas-treatment plants. Its account supports a dated distinction between affected facilities; it does not establish their condition at the October 2026 cutoff. [s3]
